clue.text: Marsh the artist is no rolling stone

indicators.note: the artist is found within the moss, so 'is' here places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a rolling stone gathers no moss, so moss is what a stone that stays put collects
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: A painter who settles in the fens and stops wandering about.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no moss' turns 'no rolling stone' into MOSS; 'is' puts RA inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A morass is a boggy stretch of wet ground, the same as a marsh.

clue.text: Gold ? That's money in college !

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'
L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A student surprised to find gold in an Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: Oriel is an Oxford college.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel College is one of the colleges of Oxford University.

clue.text: Angostura cocktail for old sailors

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A bitters-based drink fit for veteran seamen.
explanation.walkthrough: Angostura is the bitters, but 'cocktail' mixes its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argonauts were Jason's crew who sailed the Argo in Greek legend.

clue.text: Look at the boil !

parts.note: to look at something is to see it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook told to watch a pan come up to temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: To seethe is to bubble and churn as liquid does when heated.

clue.text: Centre bull, then time to get outside at last

indicators.note: the centre of a four-letter word is its two middle letters
time goes around the outside of the little word at, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A darts player hits the bullseye, then it is time to step outside at closing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre bull' looks like the bullseye but gives UL, the middle of 'bull'; TIME wraps AT to make TIMATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimate as an adjective means final, coming at the very end.

clue.text: Census — taker's assistant works where black market goods are

definitions.meaning: a census-taker counts, so his helper works beneath the counter
illicit goods are sold secretly, kept out of sight beneath the shop's counter

explanation.surface: A census official's helper deals in illicit goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes a census-taker as a counter, so an assistant works under him.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods sold secretly or illegally are said to be sold beneath the shop counter; and a census official is someone who counts.

clue.text: He gave us a lesson, say, in race tactics

definitions.text: He gave us a lesson, say, in race tactics

parts.words: He gave us a lesson, say, in race tactics
parts.note: in Aesop's fable the slow and steady creature beats the hare, teaching that slow and steady wins the race

explanation.surface: A coach who taught strategy for running events.
explanation.walkthrough: Aesop's fable of the hare and its slow shelled rival teaches that steady going wins.
explanation.definitionFit: The fable's winner, a slow shelled reptile, showed that persistence beats speed.

clue.text: But doesn't butter have the edge?

definitions.text: But doesn't butter have the edge?

parts.words: But doesn't butter have the edge?
parts.note: the butter substitute is not butter, and an old word for the edge or margin is the same

explanation.surface: Asking whether real butter beats a spread.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is short for margarine, the butter substitute, and is also an archaic word for a margin or edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for margarine, a spread made instead of dairy butter; also a poetic word for a brink or border.

clue.text: Not the whole truth about uncle being wild, bellicose

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other
the word truth is cut short, losing its last letter
the word uncle goes wild, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Telling only half the story about an uncle who is wild and aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the whole' drops H from TRUTH; 'being wild' makes CULEN from UNCLE, and 'about' puts TRUT around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Truculent means aggressively defiant and eager to fight.

clue.text: First man in the bob, the arch-villain!

definitions.meaning: a bob is a method of change ringing on church bells, so its first man is the leading ringer
the chief instigator of a crime or mischief

explanation.surface: A villain who once led a team of bell-ringers.
explanation.walkthrough: In bell-ringing a bob is a sequence of changes; the person leading the band of ringers is, read literally, the ring leader.
explanation.definitionFit: The leader of a gang of wrongdoers is its ringleader; the bell-ringing reading takes the word apart as the leader of the ring.

clue.text: Rioters put to flight

definitions.meaning: an old sense of the word is a disorderly mob or riotous crowd
to defeat an enemy so thoroughly that it runs

explanation.surface: Police scatter an unruly crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Rout once meant a riotous rabble, and as a verb it means to defeat and scatter an army.

clue.text: Does this settle the argument by hammering the point ?

definitions.text: Does this settle the argument by hammering the point ?

parts.words: Does this settle the argument by hammering the point ?
parts.note: a decisive argument settles a dispute, and a nail is fixed by hammering its point flat on the far side

explanation.surface: A debater wonders whether forceful repetition wins the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammering the point' sounds like insisting on an argument, but it also describes clinching a nail by bending its point over.
explanation.definitionFit: A clincher is a decisive argument, and also one who clinches nails by hammering their points.

clue.text: Dagger ruins a blouse

indicators.note: to ruin the garment is to wreck its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone slashing a blouse with a knife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dagger' is the printer's mark, not a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus is the printer's dagger sign used for footnotes or to mark doubtful text.

clue.text: Would a Cockney define him as indigent ?

definitions.text: Would a Cockney define him as indigent ?

parts.words: Would a Cockney define him as indigent ?
parts.note: said in a Cockney accent, 'Indian gent' comes out sounding like the word indigent

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Londoner would call a man poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indigent' means poor, but here it stands for a slurred 'Indian gent'. In British India a babu was a native clerk or gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Babu was a title for an Indian gentleman or clerk under British rule.

clue.text: No pain from leg broken in an eastern continent

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: taken as written
Asia is the eastern continent

indicators.note: a broken leg here has its letters scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone who breaks a leg in the East and feels nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges LEG to LGE, which goes 'in' ANASIA, after ANA.
explanation.definitionFit: Analgesia is the absence of feeling pain, often brought on by a drug.

clue.text: Went with expedition

parts.note: expedition can mean a journey but also speed, so going with expedition means going quickly

explanation.surface: Someone joined a party of explorers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' suggests a party of travellers, but its older sense is promptness or speed.
explanation.definitionFit: To hasten is to go with speed and dispatch.

clue.text: Here today, gone tomorrow

parts.note: the proverbial phrase describes something lasting only a short time

explanation.surface: A remark about something fleeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Something short-lived, lasting only a day or so, as the mayfly does.

clue.text: What Antonio called Shylock's well-won thrift

definitions.text: What Antonio called Shylock's well-won thrift

parts.words: What Antonio called Shylock's well-won thrift
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice Shylock complains that Antonio rails at his well-won thrift under this name, meaning money lent at a charge

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare question about the moneylender's earnings.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock says Antonio rails on 'my well-won thrift, which he calls' by this name: the charge on a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: The money charged for a loan, which Antonio condemned as usury.

clue.text: Clerical sort of nose a bird has?

parts.words: sort of nose a bird has?
parts.note: the fatty rump of a cooked fowl is known as the parson's nose

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of beak a bird has.
explanation.walkthrough: The parson's nose is the rump of a roast chicken; an adjective formed from that kind of nose means clerical.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to a parson, a clergyman, so of the clergy.

clue.text: Has old Kipling's elephant lost one?

indicators.note: the elephant has lost something, so a letter is removed from his name

parts.note: Hathi is the elephant in Kipling's Jungle Book
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a storybook elephant has misplaced something.
explanation.walkthrough: Hathi from The Jungle Book loses his final I (one).
explanation.definitionFit: Hath is the archaic third-person form of the verb have.

clue.text: Marks five per cent

definitions.meaning: marks or points totalled in a game or test
per cent means per hundred, and a hundred is five twenties

explanation.surface: A test result of only five per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, so five scores make a hundred: five 'per cent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scores are tallies of points, and also twenties, five of which make one hundred.

clue.text: Ring perhaps contains love note-note it not

indicators.note: one piece holds the other inside it
perhaps signals the word Ring is to be rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A wedding band hides a love letter, which goes unread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges RING to IGNR, which 'contains' O; E follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore something is to take no notice of it.

clue.text: Does announcer feel so elated, walking to the mike ?

definitions.text: Does announcer feel so elated, walking to the mike ?

parts.words: Does announcer feel so elated, walking to the mike ?
parts.note: an elated person is said to be walking ..., and an announcer at the microphone is broadcasting live

explanation.surface: A radio presenter wonders if nerves become joy at the microphone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walking' points to the phrase 'walking on air', meaning elated; a broadcaster at the mike is being transmitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Being broadcast on radio or television; and the idiom of walking on air means joyful.

clue.text: How rare our nobility !

parts.note: the nobility are those who are not commoners, and rare things are not common

explanation.surface: A lament that true aristocrats are scarce.
explanation.walkthrough: The peerage is the opposite of the commons, so its members are, word by word, not common.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncommon means rare, and nobles are by definition not of the common people.

clue.text: An attack where some may get shot

definitions.meaning: film actors are shot by cameras when working on a film set

explanation.surface: An assault where people might be gunned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' suggests gunfire but means filmed: actors work on set.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is the start of an assault; actors are filmed while working on a film set.

clue.text: Jorrocks's mount, and a different one

definitions.meaning: a horse ridden by Jorrocks, the hunting grocer of R. S. Surtees's novels
a different kind of mount, a mountain

explanation.surface: Comparing a fictional huntsman's horse with another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' first means a horse, then a mountain: Ossa is the Greek peak the giants piled Pelion on.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly and also the name of one of Jorrocks's horses.

clue.text: Undertaking to go in force

parts.note: to go in is to enter
to prise is to force open with a lever

explanation.surface: A project that involves storming in.
explanation.definitionFit: An enterprise is a venture or project someone takes on.

clue.text: Vexatious litigant of some eminence in the Hebrides ?

parts.note: Barra is an island of the Outer Hebrides
a tor is a rocky hill, an eminence

explanation.surface: A troublesome lawyer of high standing in the Scottish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eminence' suggests rank but means a hill: a TOR on BARRA, one island in the Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrator is one who habitually stirs up lawsuits and quarrels.

clue.text: A kiss perhaps gives an Italian health

definitions.meaning: a kiss is one way of greeting someone
the Italian word for health, also used as a toast

explanation.surface: A kiss on the cheek as an Italian toast.
explanation.definitionFit: A salute is a gesture of greeting such as a kiss, and the Italian for health is spelt the same.
